stories.headline: Supreme Court restores compensation for girl who lost hand to electrocution, raps High Court for relying on ‘mere suspicion’
stories.bodyText:
Supreme Court restores compensation for girl who lost hand to electrocution, raps High Court for relying on ‘mere suspicion’
Finding the appellant’s evidence unshaken and the utility’s defence weak, the court set aside the High Court judgment and restored the trial court’s decree.
New Delhi: The Supreme Court has restored a trial court order awarding Rs 8.70 lakh compensation to a Rajasthan woman who lost her right hand after coming into contact with a live electric wire as a minor, holding that an appellate court cannot reverse a well-considered decree on mere suspicion.
A bench of Justices Prashant Kumar Mishra and Shree Chandrashekhar held that once the incident was established on the preponderance of probabilities, the principle of strict liability applied to the electricity utility.
Finding the appellant’s evidence unshaken and the utility’s defence weak, the court set aside the High Court judgment and restored the trial court’s decree.
Rekha was a young girl when the incident occurred on the morning of July 15, 2011. She was walking through village Harivansh ka Pura-Pathaur ka Pura in Dholpur, when she came across 11 KV transmission lines that had loosened and were hanging barely three to four feet above the ground.
While trying to push the wires aside, she received a severe electric shock. Large parts of her body were burnt. After treatment at local hospitals failed, she was taken to Agra, where her right hand had to be amputated, leaving her permanently disabled.
She sued Jaipur Vidyut Vitran Nigam Limited (JVVNL), alleging negligence in maintaining the lines.
The trial court accepted her evidence and that of her witnesses, and in 2015 decreed Rs 8.70 lakh with 6 per cent interest.
The Rajasthan High Court, however, set aside the decree in 2024, calling the incident “unbelievable” and “suspicious.” It noted the delay in reporting the matter to police and expressed doubt that anyone could survive contact with an 11 KV line.
Disagreeing with the High Court's conclusion, the bench said, “A civil suit should be decided on the basis of evidence produced by the parties and not by merely raising a doubt on the claim made by the plaintiff.”
The bench observed that the High Court had committed “serious errors in law” by interfering “on mere ipse dixit.”
The court underlined that findings of fact recorded by the trial court should normally prevail unless vital defects are shown in the evidence. “There is no provision in law which authorises the court to disbelieve the incident without recording a finding that the witnesses were unreliable,” the bench said.

stories.headline: Congress MLA Gokul Setia writes letter in blood to Haryana CM, claims briefly detained by police
stories.deck: Responding to a question about Mr. Setia's alleged detention by police, Mr. Saini said the opposition MLA had neither been arrested nor taken into custody
stories.bodyText:
Congress Sirsa MLA Gokul Setia on Sunday (November 22, 2026) claimed he was briefly detained by police as he wanted to give Haryana Chief Minister Nayab Singh Saini a letter written in blood to highlight multiple civic issues in his constituency.
Mr. Saini, however, denied the MLA's claim.
Mr. Saini was in Sirsa to flag off the Kalanwali Youth Marathon, aimed at spreading awareness against drug abuse and encouraging youngsters to take up sports and adopt a healthy lifestyle, and to chair a meeting of the District Grievance Redressal Committee.
Mr. Setia had earlier said that he would sit at Shaheed Bhagat Singh Chowk on Sunday (November 22) morning and write a letter using his blood to draw the government's attention to the issues in his constituency.
"When people of Sirsa are shedding tears of blood, is it not my duty to stand in their support? Don't we say that we will give our blood and sweat for our people," the MLA told the media on Sunday (November 22).
"I was not raising any party slogan, I only wanted to hand over the letter to the chief minister. But I was detained by such heavy police force which they had deployed to stop me," he said.
He asked why the government was so scared that heavy police deployment was made to stop him.
There are civic issues related to canal water, blocked sewerage system and garbage, he said.
"But the government does not see the problems which people are facing," he added.
"I am only discharging my duties towards my electorate. What is the condition of Sirsa? People are facing so many problems. The drug problem has grown," the MLA claimed.
Station House Officer (City), Sirsa, Santosh Kumar, said Mr. Setia was told to write a letter with a pen.
"We only told the MLA that he can write a letter with a pen and give it to the chief minister," Mr. Kumar said on the phone.
Responding to a question about Mr. Setia's alleged detention by police, Mr. Saini said the opposition MLA had neither been arrested nor taken into custody.
The CM described the incident as a "drama".
Providing details of funds released for development works in the Sirsa constituency on the opposition MLA's request, Mr. Saini said over ₹94 lakh was released in 2024-25, over $2 crore in 2025-26 and ₹1.65 crore for 28 works in 2026-27.
He said a total of ₹4.07 crore had been released for 67 development works over the past three years on the request of the opposition legislator.

stories.headline: India retains 3rd spot in Asia power rankings despite economic dip: Report
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: India has consolidated its position as Asia's third-most powerful country, with its overall power score rising to 40.5 points in 2026, even as its relative economic capability weakened, according to the Lowy Institute's Asia Power Index.
The United States and China retained the top two positions, respectively, while India strengthened its regional influence through improvements in diplomatic standing, defence engagement, cultural reach and future resources, the report said.
Priyanka Jaiswal has four years of experience in digital journalism, news agency reporting and video production. Currently with The Times of India, she covers public policy, politics and global affairs. She is particularly drawn to human-interest stories that put people at the heart of an issue, spark awareness , and contribute to meaningful conversations.

stories.headline: 'Water safety is priority': Bisleri after food regulator declared samples 'unsafe'
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Bisleri International said on Monday that drinking water safety is a priority for the company and that it will cooperate with the regulator to address the matter through the appropriate process.
The statement came after the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (
FSSAI
) sanctioned prosecution against it over a packaged drinking water sample declared unsafe.
In a social media post, the FSSAI said a regulatory sample of "Packaged Drinking Water (other than Mineral Water)", collected from Bisleri International's premises, did not comply with the prescribed limits for bromate. The sample was declared unsafe under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
Bisleri appealed against the findings, and the sample was sent to a referral food laboratory. The laboratory also declared it unsafe, this time after detecting polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), the regulator said.
Citing violations relating to unsafe food, the FSSAI sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd.
Four other food businesses face prosecution
The regulator has also sanctioned prosecution against Vasant Masala Pvt Ltd, Tit-Bit Foods India Pvt Ltd, Mimansa Industries and Asha Confectionery.
In separate action, it suspended the licences of Urmi Lifesciences LLP and Gaur Ayurvedic Store for non-compliance with food safety rules. It also ordered Asha Confectionery to recall its pre-packaged chocolate-filled cookies after they were found unsafe.
FSSAI steps up enforcement
The action comes as the FSSAI intensifies enforcement against food business operators and e-commerce companies this calendar year. The regulator has also stepped up scrutiny of energy drink and alcoholic beverage manufacturers.

briefs.headline: Why clock starts ticking for cops as soon as a person is detained
briefs.bodyText:
After police pick up a person, they have exactly 24 hours to produce them before a magistrate. SC has made it clear the deadline starts at the point of detention — not when the arrest is recorded — and exceeding it amounts to a violation of fundamental rights. 
Sunil Baghel
 explains.
Supreme Court
's order on detention without prompt production before a magistrate speaks to one of the most fundamental rights - the right to freedom of movement. This is significant because this deadline has often been violated by delay in recording an arrest.
The top court has clarified that only the time needed to travel from the place of arrest to the magistrate's court to produce a suspect can be excluded from the timeframe. Time spent in questioning, searches, seizures or other legal formalities must count towards the deadline.
The court, in fact, also went a step further and clarified that sticking to the 24-hour window does not automatically make detention reasonable.
In plain English, a suspect must not be held in custody unnecessarily just because police have 24 hours to produce him before a magistrate. They must justify every hour of curtailment of a suspect's freedom of movement and magistrates must examine how long a person was held and whether that period was justified.
The Nov 5 order followed appeals by three men accused in a case involving the alleged transportation of over 60kg of contraband drugs in Tripura. A bench of Justices Ujjal Bhuyan and Atul S Chandurkar held that their detention violated Art 22(2) of the Constitution and Sec 58 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023 and set aside Tripura High Court's order rejecting their bail pleas.
Customs officials had taken the men into custody on Sept 29, 2025 and their arrests were formally recorded the next morning. They were produced before a magistrate more than 24 hours after they were first detained (see box).
When does 24-hr period begin?
Art 22(2) of the Constitution says an arrested person has to be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours. Detention beyond 24 hours requires a magistrate's authority. SC said the clock starts when a suspect is detained and their freedom is restricted, that is, "when his liberty is effectively curtailed".
There is no constitutional basis, it said, for excluding time spent on investigation, interrogation, or legal formalities from the mandated 24 hours.
The court also referred to Sec 58 of BNSS, which reflects the restriction in Sec 57 of the earlier Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), requiring detention to last no longer than is reasonable in the circumstances, even within the 24-hour limit.
What SC said
Additional solicitor general Raghavendra P Shankar, representing the Union govt, said the intervening hours before they were produced before a magistrate had been taken up by mandatory procedures like searches, seizures, preparing documents, questioning the accused, etc. He argued that arrest memos could be prepared only after the initial investigation. Until then, they were temporarily restrained to allow the search and seizure process to be completed.
The govt relied on Rule 3(4) of NDPS Rules, 2022, which requires seized substances to be classified, weighed, packaged and numbered in the presence of search witnesses and the person from whom they were recovered. The govt argued that the time taken for these necessary steps could not be treated as detention following arrest.
The bench examined earlier judgments on what amounts to arrest and custody, including a March 1980 SC judgment that held a person is in custody as soon as he is under the control of an investigating agency or an authority with powers to restrain him. Apart from citing these judgments in support of the accused, SC also rejected three HC decisions relied on by the govt, including Kannan vs State of Tamil Nadu (2026) that held that time spent on mandatory NDPS procedures before formal arrest could be excluded from the 24-hour calculation.
SC instead said that search and seizure procedures did not prevent timely production before a magistrate. They could continue after production and authorisation of judicial custody.
Why 24-hr safegaurd matters
The judgment linked prompt production before a magistrate to protection against custodial violence. It cited a Dec 1980 SC judgment - against the backdrop of the Bhagalpur blinding incidents involving prisoners - that said the 24-hour requirement allowed judicial authorities to keep a check on police investigations.
The bench also referred to the D K Basu case - that highlighted custodial violence and the practice of questioning suspects without formally recording their arrests, in which SC issued arrest safeguards in mid-90s. The latest judgment recalled earlier judicial concerns about people arrested without warrants being tortured to extract information, recover property or obtain confessions. It also cited an SC ruling in an Enforcement Directorate case, which held that a breach of Art 22(2) makes an arrest invalid and requires the court hearing the bail plea to release the accused.
Can bail rules override rights?
The court also examined Sec 37 of NDPS Act, which sets strict conditions for bail in cases involving commercial quantities of drugs. Tripura High Court had relied on an April 2026 ruling by a two-judge SC bench that held the two conditions under Sec 37 must be met before bail could be granted in such cases.
Share your thoughts in the comments
Be respectful · TOI community guidelines
The latest Supreme Court ruling questioned the suggestion that the right to a speedy trial under Art 21 must operate within the framework of Sec 37. It relied on the landmark Feb 2021 decision in Union of India vs KA Najeeb, where a three-judge SC bench recognised that strict provisions in special laws could not override fundamental rights under Art 21. It also made clear that NDPS procedures could not weaken the protection against unlawful detention under Art 22(2). In this case, the court found that the unexplained 18-hour gap between the end of search and seizure and the formal arrests was unreasonable under Sec 58 of BNSS, which states that "no police officer shall detain a person arrested without a warrant in custody for longer than is reasonable under the circumstances".

briefs.headline: India, China hold 10-day talks to ease LAC tensions in Arunachal Pradesh
briefs.deck: The talks focused on establishing engagement protocols, preventing face-offs and misunderstandings between troops deployed along the frontier, and maintaining open communication channels
briefs.bodyText:
India and China have concluded a second round of Corps Commander-level talks aimed at easing tensions along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in Arunachal Pradesh and putting in place measures to prevent friction between troops deployed along the frontier ahead of the onset of harsh winter conditions.
Sources in the Ministry of Defence confirmed that the closely guarded discussions, which began on November 8, 2026, a day after Deepavali, continued for nearly 10 days, with a short break in between. The talks were described as cordial, though it remains unclear whether the measures discussed will be implemented on the ground before winter sets in fully.
Lieutenant-General Girish Kalia, General Officer Commanding of the Army’s III Corps, also known as the Spear Corps, led the Indian delegation. The formation is headquartered at Rangapahar near Dimapur in Nagaland. His Chinese counterpart and other military officers participated in the discussions. An official from the Ministry of External Affairs was also present.
The latest round of talks primarily focused on establishing engagement protocols between the two sides, preventing face-offs and misunderstandings between troops deployed along the frontier, maintaining open communication channels and reducing tensions in the eastern sector. Both countries have deployed substantial numbers of troops in the region.
Harsh winter
The discussions assume significance as winter conditions along the LAC in Arunachal Pradesh can become extremely severe, posing considerable challenges to troop sustenance, movement and logistical support. Any delay in implementing the measures discussed could complicate the situation on the ground as temperatures fall and access to forward areas becomes increasingly difficult.
The second round follows the first Corps Commander-level meeting, held on September 6 and 7, 2026, at the Wacha-Damai Border Personnel Meeting (BPM) point in the Kibithoo sector. Wacha is India’s easternmost border personnel meeting point.
The first meeting was convened following reports of tensions in the Taksing area of Upper Subansiri district in Arunachal Pradesh, where troops from the two sides had reportedly come face to face.
The military-level engagement comes amid renewed diplomatic efforts by New Delhi and Beijing to stabilise bilateral relations. In August 2026, National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, the Special Representatives for boundary negotiations between the two countries, held talks in Beijing.
The situation along the Arunachal Pradesh frontier also came into focus in October 2026, when Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) Director-General Shatrujeet Kapur, days before his retirement, said Indian and Chinese troops had faced off at multiple locations in the State.

briefs.headline: Lost to PAK, now what? How IND A can reach Asia Cup Rising Stars semi-finals
briefs.deck: India A suffered a 48-run loss to Pakistan A in the ACC Men's Asia Cup Rising Stars tournament. Their semi-final hopes depend on the outcome of their upcoming match against the United Arab Emirates. A win against UAE will secure India A's qualification for the next round. The team is competing closely with Nepal for a semi-final spot.
briefs.bodyText:
India A suffered a 48-run defeat against Pakistan A in their ACC Men's Asia Cup Rising Stars 2026 Group B clash at the West End Park International Cricket Stadium in Doha on Sunday. The defeat has put their semi-final hopes under pressure, but they are still very much in the race for a place in the last four.
Tilak Varma-led India A have one more group match to play. They will take on the United Arab Emirates (UAE) on November 24, with a victory enough to secure their qualification.
Pakistan A, on the other hand, have qualified for the semi-finals after winning both their matches (vs UAE and India).
Only the top two teams from Group B will progress to the semi-finals, scheduled for November 26 and 27.
Asia Cup Rising Stars: Where do India A stand in the points table?
Pakistan A lead Group B with four points from two matches. India A and Nepal have two points each, while the UAE are at the bottom without a win and are out of the semi-final race.
Nepal kept their hopes alive with a six-wicket victory over the UAE earlier on Sunday. Pakistan A's win over India A took them into the semifinal.
Asia Cup Rising Stars 2026: Group B points table
India A's positive net run rate of +2.580 gives them a major advantage over Nepal and could prove decisive if the teams finish with the same number of points.
Asia Cup Rising Stars: How can India A qualify for the semi-finals?
India A still have multiple ways to reach the last four. Their match against the UAE will be particularly important.
Here are the possible outcomes:1. India A beat UAE and Pakistan A beat Nepal
This is the most straightforward route for India A. India A win against the UAE will take them to four points and guarantee a semi-final spot. 
The result of the Pakistan A-Nepal match will not affect their qualification.
2. India A beat UAE and Nepal beat Pakistan A
If Nepal upset Pakistan A, India A, Pakistan A and Nepal will all finish with four points.
In that case, net run rate will decide the final standings. India A will be in a strong position because of their 306-run victory over Nepal earlier in the tournament. Their superior net run rate makes them favourites to progress.
3. India A vs UAE match is washed out and Pakistan A beat Nepal
A washout will earn India A one point, taking their total to three.
They will still qualify if Pakistan A defeat Nepal. Nepal will remain on two points, while India A will finish with three and secure the second qualification spot.
4. UAE beat India A and Pakistan A beat Nepal
A defeat against the UAE will make things complicated, but it will not automatically end India's campaign.
Pakistan A will finish with six points, while India A, Nepal and the UAE will all have two points each.
India A will have the advantage because of their much better net run rate. However, the margin of defeat against the UAE will be crucial in deciding whether they progress.
5. UAE beat India A and Nepal beat Pakistan A
This is the one result combination that will knock India A out of the tournament.
Pakistan A and Nepal will finish with four points each, while India A will be stuck on two. Pakistan A and Nepal will then take the two semi-final spots, ending India's campaign.

briefs.headline: 'No wilful absence:' Supreme Court orders reinstatement of CRPF constable sacked for overstaying leave
briefs.bodyText:
'No wilful absence:' Supreme Court orders reinstatement of CRPF constable sacked for overstaying leave
Mithilesh Kumar Pathak, then posted with the 54th Battalion in Anantnag, Jammu and Kashmir, was granted casual leave from September 21 to October 12, 2000, on account of his wife’s illness.
New Delhi: The Supreme Court has said unauthorised absence does not always mean wilful absence as it directed the reinstatement of a Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) constable who had been removed from service for overstaying leave by 99 days.
The court held that the penalty was “grossly disproportionate” and that the authorities had rejected his medical explanation on mere conjectures.
A bench of Justices Satish Chandra Sharma and Nongmeikapam Kotiswar Singh set aside a 2010 Patna High Court division bench order that had restored the constable’s removal.
The apex court revived the single judge’s 2007 decision that had quashed the dismissal and ordered the force to take him back.
Mithilesh Kumar Pathak, then posted with the 54th Battalion in Anantnag, Jammu and Kashmir, was granted casual leave from September 21 to October 12, 2000, on account of his wife’s illness.
He reported back only on January 19, 2001. He explained that he himself had fallen ill with infective hepatitis in his village in Bihar’s Munger district and submitted medical prescriptions, lab reports, medicine bills and a fitness certificate.
A departmental enquiry found him guilty of unauthorised absence and disobedience of two letters asking him to return. The enquiry officer discarded the medical papers mainly because they lacked hospital registration numbers and appeared written with the same pen, inferring fabrication. Pathak was removed from service in March 2001.
The Supreme Court said unauthorised absence is not always the same as wilful absence.
“The circumstances in which an employee remained absent, the explanation furnished, and the material supporting that explanation must be considered,” the bench observed.
It held that the medical documents could not be rejected without any verification from the treating doctor or pharmacy. Similarity of ink or absence of an outdoor patient number, by themselves, did not prove forgery.
While acknowledging the need for discipline in a force deployed in a sensitive area, the court ruled that removal for a 99-day overstay was unduly harsh.
“The punishment imposed must satisfy the requirement of proportionality,” it said, adding that the penalty shocked the conscience in the facts of the case.
The court directed Pathak’s immediate reinstatement with 50 per cent back wages for the period he remained out of service and all consequential benefits.

briefs.headline: Canadian homebuyer backs out of C$18m deal; court revives C$4.26m damages award
briefs.deck: A Canadian judge has cancelled a C$4.26 million damages order against a buyer who failed to complete an C$18 million home purchase. The property was later sold for C$14.3 million. The buyer challenged the original judgment, disputing the contract conditions and the compensation claimed by the seller. Although he waited more than three years to approach the court, the judge allowed him to defend…
briefs.bodyText:
A Canadian judge has given a buyer another chance to defend himself in a dispute over an C$18 million property deal that fell through in 2021. The decision cancels a C$4.26 million order against Stephen Brown, who had agreed to buy the property from Rakesh Dhunna but did not complete the purchase.
Dhunna later sold the property for C$14.3 million, which was C$3.7 million less than the agreed price. He took Brown to court and secured an order for C$4,262,369.40 in compensation after the buyer failed to respond to the case.
Brown eventually approached the court to challenge the order. He argued that he had reasons to defend himself and also questioned how the seller's losses had been calculated.
In a decision dated March 25, Justice Stephens of the British Columbia Supreme Court allowed Brown to contest the claim. The judge cancelled the earlier orders and gave him 30 days to file his response.
Property sold for C$14.3 million
According to the informationa available in the 
judgment
, Brown and Dhunna signed the purchase agreement on April 17, 2021. The agreed price was C$18 million, but the sale did not go through.
Dhunna filed a case against Brown on September 16. Brown received the legal notice five days later but did not respond within the required 21 days.
As a result, Dhunna obtained a court order in November in his favour. 
The property was eventually sold in April 2023 for C$14.3 million.
Dhunna then sought compensation for the difference between the original sale price and the amount received from the later sale. He also included expenses incurred while holding the property. On July 18, 2023, the court ordered Brown to pay C$4,262,369.40.
Buyer disputes seller's losses
When Brown challenged the order, he questioned why Dhunna had not accepted an earlier offer for the property. He told the court that the seller had received an offer of C$14.8 million in February 2022 but did not accept it. The property was sold for C$14.3 million in April 2023.
Brown argued that accepting the earlier offer would have reduced the amount claimed against him by C$500,000. He also questioned the expenses of about C$562,369 that Dhunna had included for keeping the property until it was sold.
Buyer explains why he did not respond
Brown did not ask the court to cancel the earlier order until June 30, 2025, more than three years after it was issued. He had represented himself in the case until April 2025, when he hired a lawyer.
He told the court that he had not understood the legal process or realised that he could ask for the earlier decision to be reconsidered. He believed the property deal was no longer active and said he was also dealing with personal and financial difficulties.
Brown's affidavit mentioned the deaths of his father in Saskatchewan and his wife's niece in Oregon during this period.
The judge found that Brown had not deliberately ignored the original case. However, the court also noted that he had waited a long time before taking steps to challenge the order. His personal circumstances did not fully explain why he had allowed so much time to pass.
Dispute over purchase conditions
Brown also raised questions about the conditions attached to the original property agreement. Dhunna relied on an addendum dated April 23, 2021, which he said showed that Brown had agreed to remove certain conditions from the deal.
Brown acknowledged that the signature on the document appeared to be his but said he did not remember signing it. He denied agreeing to remove the conditions. The judge also noted that Dhunna's signature was missing from the document, although there was a space for it.
The court did not decide whether the conditions had been removed. However, the judge found that the disagreement needed to be examined further because it could affect whether Brown was required to complete the purchase.

briefs.headline: Mary Sherman Morgan developed fuel that launched America's first satellite
briefs.bodyText:
Born on a small farm near Ray, North Dakota, Mary Sherman Morgan went on to become the only woman among roughly 900 rocket scientists at North American Aviation, where she led the development of a powerful rocket fuel called Hydyne. A chemistry student whose university education was interrupted by the Second World War, Morgan put her expertise to work designing explosives before moving into the aerospace industry. Her fuel was later used in the first stage of the Jupiter-C rocket that launched Explorer 1 into orbit on 31 January 1958, marking America's first successful satellite launch.
Mary Sherman Morgan’s work at North American Aviation
Morgan spent the war years designing explosives for the military at Plum Brook Ordnance Works. The facility played a significant role in wartime production, with Prairie Public NewsRoom reporting that the plant produced one billion pounds of munitions during the Second World War.
After the war, Morgan moved into the aerospace industry, securing a position with North American Aviation, a company based in California. Her experience in chemistry and explosives proved useful in her new role, where she worked on calculating the performance of rocket fuels.
According to Prairie Public NewsRoom, she was promoted to the position of Theoretical Performance Specialist. She was the only woman among nearly 900 engineers working in the field and was also one of the few employees who did not hold a college degree.
Hydyne: The powerful rocket fuel developed by Mary Sherman Morgan
North American Aviation had secured a contract to develop powerful rocket fuels capable of propelling rockets into Earth's orbit as the United States worked towards launching satellites. Morgan's expertise and experience led to her being appointed technical lead of the project.
According to Physics Today, Morgan was the only woman among roughly 900 rocket scientists at the company and had been named technical lead of the rocket-fuel project. Her work resulted in Hydyne, a more powerful propellant developed for the American space programme.
Hydyne was a mixture comprising 60 per cent unsymmetrical dimethylhydrazine and 40 per cent diethylenetriamine. The fuel was developed to improve rocket performance and was subsequently used in the first stage of the Jupiter-C rocket.
Mary Sherman Morgan’s fuel powered the launch of Explorer 1
Morgan's work on Hydyne became particularly significant during the United States' efforts to place its first successful satellite into orbit. According to Prairie Public NewsRoom, the new fuel powered three Jupiter-C rockets and helped launch America's first satellite on 31 January 1958.
The satellite, Explorer 1, was successfully launched into orbit, marking the beginning of the United States' participation in the Space Age. Hydyne was used for the first stage of America's first successful satellite launch in 1958.
Mary Sherman Morgan’s contribution to America’s space programme
Despite her involvement in developing the fuel, Morgan remained reserved about her professional achievements and rarely discussed her work. Physics Today noted that she received little credit for her accomplishments throughout her life.
Morgan's contribution was acknowledged by former colleagues after her death. At her funeral, a former co-worker told her son that she had single-handedly saved America's space programme. Former colleagues shared similar sentiments with her family at the funeral.
Morgan was married to George Richard Morgan, an engineering graduate of the California Institute of Technology, and the couple had four children. Her son, George Morgan, later wrote a play and a book about her life and work, helping bring attention to her role in the development of American rocket technology.
Mary Sherman Morgan died on 4 August 2004, aged 82. Her work on Hydyne remains part of the history of the development of the rocket technology used to launch Explorer 1, America's first successful satellite.

briefs.headline: 'Rehire Jensen': Trump backs ex Nvidia CEO's return amid fresh China spy agency claims
briefs.bodyText:
US president 
Donald Trump
 has once again voiced support for Jensen Huang’s possible return as Nvidia’s chief executive, saying he hoped the company’s board would “rehire” him. His remarks come amid fresh reports that Alice Huang remained in contact with an official from China’s spy agency for more than a year during her reported relationship with the former Nvidia CEO.
“I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang. It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the USA,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social.
The New York Times had earlier reported on Sunday that the Chinese businesswoman was in contact with an officer from China’s Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 until the autumn of 2026. The report cited people familiar with intelligence assessments describing the encounters.
Alice Huang previously led Singapore-based Megaspeed International, an important Nvidia customer that once accounted for billions of dollars in chip sales. US authorities have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 over concerns that it smuggled Nvidia’s advanced artificial intelligence chips to China, Reuters reported.
However, US officials have repeatedly said they have not reached a conclusion on whether Alice Huang spied for China. 
US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton reiterated that the matter remained under investigation.
“Attorney General Blanche has been very clear that this is a matter under investigation, both Ms Huang and her company, for various matters,” Clayton told CNN’s State of the Union programme. “And I’m going to let that investigation play out.”
The controversy intensified after an October 29 report by the New York Times, which triggered scrutiny of Jensen Huang’s personal and professional associations. He resigned on November 12, following revelations about extramarital relationships, including one involving Alice Huang.
Trump had earlier indicated that he would not oppose Jensen Huang’s return. “I think he learned a big lesson. I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that,” he told reporters on November 16.
“He could return. There’s a big group of people that would like him to return,” Trump added.
In an interview with Fox News broadcast on Wednesday, he said he had not heard that Alice Huang was a spy.
“I haven’t heard that,” Trump said when asked whether the affair posed a national security threat. “I haven’t heard that she was a spy.”
“It was a woman. It was a pretty woman. And any pretty woman that comes from China, they consider her to be a spy. I haven't heard that she was a spy. She was a businesswoman who bought chips,” he said.
He also described Jensen Huang as a “brilliant man” and said the issue had only come up briefly during his conversation with Chinese president Xi Jinping.
Trump had expressed openness to Jensen Huang’s reinstatement on November 16, telling reporters: “I think he learned a big lesson. I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that.”
“He could return. There’s a big group of people that would like him to return,” he added.

stories.headline: BMTC Central Store audit flags Rs 4-crore irregularities; FIR filed against 21 over missing spare parts in Bengaluru
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 Fake gate entries, forged signatures, cloned invoices, and backdated computer records allegedly used to conceal thousands of missing spare parts have come to light in an internal audit of the BMTC Central Store-1. The audit has uncovered alleged financial irregularities exceeding Rs 4 crore over five years, with 21 people, including serving and retired officials and a private supplier, named in a police case.
Wilson Garden police registered an FIR Friday following a complaint by Parimala L Nayik, a security and vigilance officer with Bangalore Metropolitan Transport Corporation (BMTC). The alleged irregularities involve employees of Central Store-1 in Shantinagar and span the period between April 1, 2021, and Nov 20, 2026.
Following tip-offs, BMTC constituted a special committee to examine purchase orders, invoices, stock verification reports and payment records. Its inquiry and questioning of staff is said to have uncovered six categories of irregularities.
In Jan 2026, Gajanana Engineering Works allegedly colluded with store employees to raise bills worth Rs 2.4 lakh for steering locks, ignition assemblies, and 24V point sets that were never delivered. 
Assistant store keeper Nagaraja, junior assistant N Ashok, assistant store keeper Shilpa AL and store superintendent ML Chaya allegedly facilitated the transaction. Despite the absence of gate-entry records, fake security seals were stamped on documents and security personnel’s signatures forged.
In Feb 2026, employees allegedly manipulated BMTC’s Inventory Management System (IMS) to show receipt of spare parts that had never been delivered. Invoice numbers originally issued by Urs Auto Links, through Setco Auto Systems Pvt Ltd, were allegedly copied to create fake entries showing supplies to private firm ISHA Ventures. The attempted fraud amounted to Rs 8.8 lakh.
The audit also found discrepancies in supplies by GS and Company.The firm billed five boxes containing 1,308 rolls of one-inch 2K masking tape at 30 metres per roll. Physical verification found that 720 rolls measured only around 24.5 metres each, causing an alleged loss of Rs 2.4 lakh.
The same firm raised four invoices between May and Sept 2025 for 65 industrial first-aid boxes worth Rs 66,585. Although officials signed off on their receipt, an inspection in April 2026 found only 42 boxes, of which 37 contained expired and unusable medicines.
Another alleged procurement fraud involved 400 low air-pressure switches ordered from Bani Auto Industries through Gajanana Engineering Works between March and July 2025. The supplier allegedly delivered cheaper panel/ignition switches instead. Store personnel certified 300 switches without proper inspection, resulting in the release of Rs 2.1 lakh. The remaining 100 switches had been rejected by the divisional mechanical engineer, who marked the June 17, 2025, invoice as “wrong supply rejected”. However, employees allegedly recreated the bill with a July 19 date, generated a receiving voucher for Rs 69,030, and forwarded it for payment.
The biggest discrepancy involved 2,820 spare parts meant for Tata, Leyland and Eicher buses, valued at more than Rs 3.9 crore. Shortages were detected across five financial years, from 2021-22 to 2025-26. According to the complaint, officials exploited an older computer system module called “material issue without indent” under the “master” head to conceal the missing inventory. They allegedly generated fabricated, backdated issue receipts claiming the components had been distributed to various BMTC depots over the preceding 5-6 years, making the official records tally with the available stock.
The FIR names 21 accused: Nagaraja, N Ashok, Shilpa AL, Vishwanath LD, RM Bantanoorakar, Manmathan, ML Chaya, Roopa S, Anitha GR, MS Prakash, Ramesh, Vishwanath N, Prema Viraktamatha, Hemanth BR, Mohan Kumar, Lokesh CV, Krishnaveni, Vasantha Bai, Vidya V Raykar, Jagadish M, and Janaki Rama.

stories.headline: Enforcement Directorate flags malpractices in 13 KPSC recruitment notifications, submits status report to Karnataka high court
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru: The Directorate of Enforcement (ED) has flagged alleged large-scale malpractices in 13 Karnataka Public Service Commission (KPSC) recruitment notifications, citing evidence of OMR sheet tampering, missing CCTV footage, irregular selection committee meetings, and cash-for-jobs deals.
The agency has sought further action from the 
special investigation team
 (SIT), which is probing irregularities in KPSC recruitments.
In a status report submitted to Karnataka high court, ED has detailed alleged irregularities during the tenures of former KPSC chairman Sahukar S Shivashankarappa and suspended IAS officer Gyanendra Kumar Gangwar.The court Saturday directed the jurisdictional police to file an FIR.
Among the examinations under scrutiny is the one for assistant executive engineer (RDPR department) recruitment in 2022-23. A KPSC sub-committee, in a report dated Jan 23, 2025, found OMR sheet tampering and discrepancies, besides missing or incorrect CCTV footage. It also flagged a meeting held on Jan 31, 2024, without the required quorum or the chairman, during which the final selection list was approved.
According to ED, Gangwar admitted to OMR tampering involving 10 candidates, while an individual named Dayanand alleged that Rs 30 lakh had been demanded for selection.
The KAS gazetted probationers exam-2023 has also come under the scanner. Material seized from retired assistant secretary Prakash T reportedly indicated that Rs 1.5 crore had been collected in exchange for awarding higher marks in the KAS Mains exam held on May 2, 2025.
The agency also cited statements and admissions relating to over Rs 1 crore in cash and cheques worth Rs 30 lakh allegedly given to RJ Mahesh Kumar, personal assistant to the controller of examinations. Statements recorded during investigation are said to have indicated that illegal gratification generally ranged from Rs 40 lakh to Rs 1 crore, with higher amounts charged for KAS selections.
Further irregularities were flagged in the motor vehicle inspector (MVI) exam 2016 and the assistant engineer recruitment for BBMP and the water resources department in 2024.
Sources said handwritten notes seized from Prakash recorded pending illegal gratification of Rs 5 lakh to Rs 10 lakh per candidate in the MVI recruitment. The amounts were allegedly to be routed through Mahesh Kumar to Gangwar and others. The notes also contained cash details and entries allegedly linked to candidates selected for assistant engineer posts in BBMP.
ED informed the court that it had earlier shared the findings with SIT. The court directed the jurisdictional police to register cases based on the information provided by the agency and transfer them to SIT for investigation.

stories.headline: BMTC spare parts ‘scam’: FIR against 21 officials, employees and suppliers over alleged ₹3.97-crore fraud
stories.bodyText:
An alleged scam involving the supply of spare parts to the Bengaluru Metropolitan Transport Corporation (BMTC) has come to light, with Wilson Garden police registering an FIR against 21 officials and employees, along with companies supplying spare parts to the corporation.
The complaint was filed by an officer attached to the BMTC Vigilance Department.
According to the complaint, forged documents were allegedly created in the names of five companies claiming that 2,820 spare parts had been supplied to BMTC buses, even though the materials were allegedly not delivered.
The alleged fraud amounts to nearly ₹3.98 crore, the complaint said. The case was registered on November 20.
Although spare parts were allegedly never supplied, records were created to show that the materials had been received.
The complaint further alleges that BMTC’s Central Office had no corresponding records confirming the receipt of the materials. However, seals of the central office and forged signatures of vigilance personnel were allegedly affixed to the goods invoices to make the transactions appear genuine.
Fake warehouse-receipt documents and receipts were also allegedly generated. Signatures of a retired divisional mechanical engineer were reportedly forged on these documents.

stories.headline: Traffic management, not enforcement, will be our priority: Bengaluru Traffic Commissioner
stories.deck: Hemant M. Nimbalkar says officers must focus on managing traffic rather than enforcement, and that no vehicle should be stopped unless there is a visible violation
stories.bodyText:
The restructuring of the Bengaluru City Police administration has also resulted in a dedicated Commissioner for Bengaluru Traffic Police (BTP), even as the five Commissioners will oversee traffic in their respective jurisdictions at the local level. This, it is argued, will bring together ground-level implementation and city-level planning.
Hemant M. Nimbalkar, the new Traffic Commissioner, Bengaluru, speaks to The Hindu about his plans to tackle the city’s notorious traffic gridlocks. Edited excerpts:
The Hindu: Bengaluru’s traffic congestion is notorious and you have the challenge to beat it. What will be your first move?
Hemant Nimbalkar: We see very few of our officers on the road and this needs to change. Henceforth, even senior officials including Deputy Commissioners of Police (DCPs) will have to be on the roads during peak hours. A junction chart, like a beat system for the law and order police, will be drawn up and this will serve as a roster for officers to take turns managing traffic at junctions. Our office needs to be the road.
TH: Will this also mean an increase in contact enforcement? Citizens are already complaining about harassment by the police on the road.
HN: No. Officers have to focus on managing traffic first, not enforcement. No vehicle should be stopped unless there is a visible violation. For instance, anyone riding without a helmet or driving on the wrong side of the road has to be stopped because it is a safety issue. The practice of stopping vehicles at officers’ will will stop.
TH: There has been an argument that the enforcement is not punitive enough to create deterrence among violators. How will you address that?
HN: Traffic violations that endanger human lives will be dealt with seriously.
TH: There are concerns over dual reporting structure for traffic management in the new setup. Will this create any confusion?
HN: There is no confusion. Traffic management is both local and pan-city at the same time. Each of the five commissionerates has traffic divisions that will be monitored by the respective Commissioners. This decentralisation will help the city with more pragmatic local solutions. But traffic is also dynamic, and congestion in one part has an impact on another. That is where city-level leadership, the Traffic Management Centre and the deployment of technology come in.
TH: What are your plans to decongest the city?
HN: Congestion cannot be beaten through traffic management alone. But from our side, we will take a holistic approach to identify the reasons for congestion at a given point. Traffic personnel standing at a signal are not in charge of just that signal, but a stretch of 300–500 metres before that. The move to station senior officers at junctions during peak hours will help us better understand the reasons for congestion at any point. For instance, illegal parking, driving on one-way roads and other violations also contribute to congestion. Better enforcement along the stretch will help us ease congestion to some extent.
For this, we need a combination of artificial intelligence, big data analytics, human intelligence and human effort, which will be my approach to managing Bengaluru’s traffic.
TH: There was a plan to stop all heavy vehicles outside the city to improve traffic flow within Bengaluru. Will this be pursued?
HN: All heavy vehicles cannot be stopped from entering the city. However, we need to develop a filtering mechanism to distinguish vehicles carrying essential commodities from those transporting other goods and allow the former to enter the city. For other vehicles, a time-based entry and exit plan can be explored. We need to strike a balance between what should and should not be permitted, particularly during peak hours.
TH: Civic works disrupting traffic has been a major issue in the city. How do you plan to address this?
HN: We will try to streamline coordination with other agencies. We will look at establishing common ground to ensure that infrastructure works are carried out with minimal disruption to traffic. Practical solutions will be explored. We cannot stop development work. Road works, though they may cause immediate inconvenience, are the only way to ease congestion in the long run. We need to work around this. With the Traffic Commissioner also being a member of the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA), coordination is only expected to get better.

briefs.headline: Bengaluru gym trainer killed in hit-and-run on Silk Board Outer Ring Road, driver absconds
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 A 32-year-old gym trainer was killed after a speeding car rammed into him while he was standing beside his scooter on Silk Board Outer Ring Road in Madiwala’s Teachers Colony around 12.30am Sunday. The impact flung him into the air, leaving him with severe head injuries. The driver fled the scene without stopping.
The deceased, Shyam Eliz, a resident of Pragathinagar near Electronics City, worked at a gym in Koramangala.
According to the preliminary investigation, Eliz was returning home from Koramangala on his scooter when he reached a stretch in Teachers Colony where the BWSSB had completed some work and placed stones to block traffic. Instead of taking an alternative route, he rode between the stones and stopped on the ORR. He was standing beside his scooter when the car hit him.
The impact threw Eliz onto the service road. Passersby alerted the police and rushed him to a nearby hospital, where doctors declared him brought dead. The car driver fled without stopping to help.
Madiwala traffic police registered a case based on a complaint filed by Eliz’s father. However, CCTV footage from the spot is unclear. “We can only see that a car hit Eliz, but the make of the vehicle cannot be ascertained from the footage. Efforts are on to trace the absconding driver,” a police officer said.

briefs.headline: Volunteers mark 100th #IamBengaluru Parks initiative event with sapling planting at Mesthripalya Lake
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru
: From college students to resident welfare association (RWA) leaders and long-time residents, citizens came together at Mesthripalya Lake in Koramangala Sunday to plant and water saplings, marking the 100th event of the #IamBengaluru – Volunteer for Parks initiative.
The participation of younger citizens, particularly Gen Z students, was a notable feature of the event organised by Adamya Chetana Foundation. Several activities were organised across Bengaluru as part of the initiative, including waste segregation, park clean-ups, composting, biodiversity surveys, bird walks and plantation care.
The Indian Ploggers Army conducted a jog-and-plog drive with solid waste segregation at DP Ground in JP Nagar 2nd Phase. The Naturalist School organised biodiversity surveys at Souharda Udyanavana Park in Malleswaram and a nature walk at Ullal Basthi Junjappa Park in SMV Layout.
Team Social Spotlight held a bird walk at Kasturi Nagar Lake Park and a plantation care and de-weeding activity at Thalaghattapura Park. The bird walk recorded several species, including the Asian koel, green bee-eater, pond heron, rose-ringed parakeet, Asian openbill stork and purple-rumped sunbird.
Youth for Seva organised composting and a clean-up drive at Nagarbhavi 9th Block Park, besides plogging and litter hotspot mapping at Atal Bihari Vajpayee Park in Nandini Layout. Adamya Chetana Foundation led the plantation activity at Mesthripalya Lake.
Participants speakRamalinga Reddy, minister of forest: Bengaluru has a huge population, but very few parks and playgrounds, apart from the green spaces in some BDA layouts. There are not many parks or playgrounds in revenue layouts. We have only Lalbagh and Cubbon Park as large green spaces, but they are not sufficient. We need to increase the city’s green cover. My department is making every effort to expand green spaces, and several initiatives have been taken.
Balarama Govinde, volunteer, Adamya Chetana: After staying here for more than 30 years, I can very clearly say that taking our environment seriously is the need of the hour and must be the priority. Otherwise, none of us will survive. Planting such saplings is the smallest contribution I can make to save my city, and honestly, this is not sufficient at all. However, I am very happy to see Gen Z and Gen Alpha participating in such initiatives.
Dhruv, student, RVITM: The lack of rainfall and the scorching sun and heat we are experiencing in Nov are clear indications of why we are here and why we need to keep doing what we are doing. I believe one small sapling does make a difference, and it feels really nice to be at such a place on a Sunday morning.
Sreevardhan, student, BMS College: This experience has been very nice. We get to learn a lot while planting saplings. I actually travel via Hebbal and feel very sad about the trees being cut for the tunnel project. Instead, I’d really want authorities to explore whether these trees can be relocated or transplanted, as is done in Japan and other countries.
Meena Krishna, homemaker, Thalaghattapura: If you see waste, don’t add to it. Dispose of it where it belongs, and if someone around you is littering, tell them not to. These are simple things each of us can do — and if we all do them, we can keep our lakes and surroundings clean.
Malavika, nature enthusiast, Jakkur: This was my first biodiversity survey, and it was fascinating to discover how much life exists in a relatively small urban space. We saw butterflies, spiders and birds, and I learnt how to observe and identify them more closely. It has made me want to explore and understand Bengaluru’s biodiversity better.
Deepti, software professional: Cleaning a park is only the first step; keeping it clean is the real achievement. The activity reminded me that public spaces are a collective responsibility, and that small efforts by citizens can create meaningful change. Bengaluru has given us so much, and this was one small way of giving back.

briefs.headline: Andhra Pradesh’s YS Sharmila, mother stopped by Bengaluru police near bungalow amid court order restriction

 High drama unfolded on Bagaluru Main Road Sunday evening when Andhra Pradesh Congress Committee (APCC) president YS Sharmila and her mother, YS Vijayalakshmi, were stopped by police while heading towards a family bungalow. The property is currently occupied by her brother and Yuvajana Sramika Rythu Congress Party president

.

Sharmila reportedly told the police that she had no intention of entering the bungalow and would merely pass by it before proceeding to a five-star hotel on Thanisandra Main Road.

briefs.headline: Bengaluru officials remove Forum Mall tiles to restore footpath; split flyover proposed at Konanakunte Cross
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru
: Pedestrians walking past Forum Mall at Konanakunte were often forced to step onto the carriageway and navigate around a traffic island due to the absence of a continuous footpath. This is set to change, with Bengaluru South City Corporation officials removing a tiled section along the mall frontage Saturday to restore pedestrian access.
During the Ward One programme, greater Bengaluru development minister Krishna Byre Gowda was informed that the land in question was relinquished to the civic body, which has rights over the property. He directed officials to reclaim the space and make it available for public use.
The mall had tiled the portion adjoining its entrance, effectively blocking pedestrian access. Consequently, those taking a left turn towards the mall had to step onto the carriageway near the traffic island and walk along the road, exposing themselves to the risk of moving vehicles. Soon after the minister’s inspection, GBA officials removed the tiled portion on either side of the mall entrance, clearing approximately three metres of space on both sides.
Split-type flyover to decongest the junction
Meanwhile, as part of a broader traffic improvement plan for Konanakunte Cross, B-Smile has proposed a split-type flyover, with elevated stretches of approximately 600 metres on either side of the junction. The project is estimated to cost Rs 77 crore, including land acquisition, and is currently at the tendering stage. Officials have also been directed to secure a portion of Metro-owned land near Forum Mall to facilitate a free-left turn. In addition, a skywalk is being planned to improve pedestrian connectivity to the upcoming Metro station without affecting the proposed flyover.

briefs.headline: Crime prevention: Bengaluru police launch crackdown on rowdies
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 In a major crackdown on anti-social elements, Bengaluru city police conducted special verification drives, early-morning inspections and area domination operations across the city, checking activities and whereabouts of rowdy-sheeters and habitual offenders. The move came following a meeting with chief minister 
DK Shivakumar
 Friday.
In the north-east division, special inspections were conducted within the limits of Yelahanka, Sampigehalli, Bagalur, Kodigehalli and Kothanur police stations under the guidance of the commissioner of police, north.
Separately, police personnel from the Indiranagar division conducted surprise visits and inspections at the residences of prominent active rowdy-sheeters within their jurisdiction. During the drive, police verified the residential addresses, current workplaces, associates and their activities. Information was also gathered about their movements and whereabouts. They were strictly warned against indulging in unlawful activities or acts that could disturb public peace and order. Police said continuous surveillance would be maintained over their activities in the coming days and that preventive measures would continue to ensure law and order and public safety.
Meanwhile, the north division police conducted an area domination. During the operation, 374 vehicles were checked, 70 rowdy-sheeters and 24 modus operandi offenders were verified, and individuals with criminal backgrounds were kept under surveillance. Police also checked suspicious persons, established naka points in sensitive areas and conducted area patrols. Around 53 vehicles were seized.
In a significant seizure, police recovered 8.5 litres of liquor during an inspection at the residence of a rowdy-sheeter in RT Nagar police station limits. A case was registered under the Excise Act.
Special patrolling was also undertaken to crack down on drug-peddling networks, unnecessary gatherings of groups during night hours and public consumption of alcohol.

briefs.headline: Decks cleared for forfeiting copies of controversial book Basava Mantapa in Karnataka
briefs.bodyText:
With the Karnataka government finally issuing a notification to “forfeit” copies of the controversial book Basava Mantapa by NRI author Ravi Hanj on Sunday, the decks have been cleared for the implementation of the Cabinet decision taken on November 19. The notification states that copies of the book are being forfeited “to maintain public order and communal harmony”.
The notification was a legal necessity for the police to “forfeit” copies of the book under Section 98 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. However, the three-day delay in the government issuing the notification led to copies of the book being sold like hot cakes over the last three days in Bengaluru.
This comes a day after the author, Mr. Hanj, who had claimed on social media that he was in the United States after the controversy erupted, was tracked down at Kochi airport while allegedly trying to leave the country. He was detained and served a notice on Saturday to appear before the Bengaluru City Police on November 24.
Books to be forfeited
Senior police officials said the police would begin forfeiting copies of the book, both in print and digital formats, across the State from Monday. The book cannot be sold henceforth. Any magistrate may also issue search warrants for the purpose.
Public order and communal harmony
The notification, issued by Archana M.S., Deputy Secretary (Law and Order), Home Department, Karnataka, on Sunday, quoted the Cabinet’s decision and a proposal by the Director General and Inspector General of Police (DG&IGP), Karnataka Police, seeking issuance of the notification.
The proposal by the State police cited protests against the book across Karnataka and said it was necessary to forfeit copies of the book to “preserve public order and communal harmony”. It further stated that the book contained “defamatory and misleading content about the cultural icon of the State, Basavanna”. “Those who read the book may be misled about the real history. It is important to protect the sanctity of real history. We should also ensure that society, the community and future generations know the real history and that of Basavanna,” the notification further quoted from the proposal submitted by the DG&IGP, Karnataka Police.

briefs.headline: Helmetless riding cases in Bengaluru more than double compared to 2025, touch 42.90 lakh
briefs.deck: A senior BTP officer told The Hindu that the number of cases had doubled because violations had been booked with zero tolerance through contactless enforcement over the last five months
briefs.bodyText:
A whopping 42.90 lakh challans were issued for riding without a helmet in Bengaluru in the first 10 months of 2026, more than double the 20.22 lakh cases booked in the whole of 2025.
Data from the Bengaluru Traffic Police (BTP), reviewed by The Hindu in the wake of a helmetless rider dying in a road accident recently, showed that cases of riding without a helmet increased by 112.47% in 2026 compared with the total number of cases booked in 2025. However, cases in 2025 had dropped by 25% from 2024 as the year saw only contactless enforcement.
Last week, a 19-year-old degree student was killed and an 18-year-old boy sustained severe head injuries after their two-wheeler crashed into a divider on Santhanur Road, North Bengaluru. Neither of them was wearing a helmet.
The data also shows that cases of pillion riders travelling without helmets have doubled, with the BTP issuing 26.22 lakh challans for the violation this year, compared with 11.27 lakh in the whole of last year.
These two violations continue to be among the traffic rules most frequently flouted by Bengaluru commuters, the data shows. Wrong parking, driving without a seat belt, jumping signals and driving or riding on the wrong side are among the other common violations.
Increased contactless enforcement
A senior BTP officer told The Hindu that the number of cases had doubled because helmetless riding violations had been booked with zero tolerance through contactless enforcement over the last five months. “Helmetless riding has become rampant in the city, and there is an immediate need to curb these cases. Contact enforcement for riding without a helmet has also been increased. However, to curb this violation, we have aggressively started issuing challans from our camera feeds,” the officer said.
The increased use of contactless enforcement for booking riding-without-helmet cases is also reflected in the data. In the first three months of 2026, the share of contactless challans dropped from 96% in the corresponding period last year to 84%. In the subsequent months, contactless bookings increased to 90%, and by October, the share had risen to over 92% this year.
Increase penalty
Another BTP official said curbing helmetless riding would not be possible unless fines were increased. “The Transport Department is exploring legal ways to increase fines for riding on footpaths, which is necessary. Similarly, riding without a helmet should also attract hefty penalties,” the officer said, adding that otherwise, shaping commuter behaviour would be difficult.
The officer further said that, along with increasing penalties, the State government should also stop frequently introducing a 50% concession on traffic challans. Such concessions make it difficult to bring about a change in commuter behaviour.

stories.headline: Oil prices fall as global market selloff weighs on sentiment; Gulf attacks limit losses
stories.bodyText:
Oil prices declined on Monday as a selloff in global financial markets spread to commodities, with concerns over the artificial intelligence sector's ability to drive economic growth weighing on investor sentiment. However, continued attacks on Gulf shipping amid the unresolved US-Israeli war against Iran limited the decline.
Brent crude futures fell 28 cents, or 0.30%, to $92.29 a barrel by 0216 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures slipped 15 cents, or 0.18%, to $83.26 a barrel.
Both benchmarks extended their losing streaks, with Brent declining 4% and WTI falling 5% last week.
The weakness in oil prices came as Asian equity markets opened lower on Monday, following a sharp selloff in global technology stocks. South Korea's tech-heavy market dropped 4%, while markets in China, Hong Kong and Australia also traded lower. In the US, the Nasdaq plunged 10% last week amid concerns over the outlook for AI-related investments.
"It’s momentum carrying (oil) down," said Mukesh Sahdev, chief oil analyst at Sydney-based XAnalysts.
However, Sahdev cautioned that attacks on shipping could eventually put upward pressure on crude prices. 
"ballast (empty) vessels counts are building in crude while laden vessels are not. This risk to flows will start to price soon."
The continuing conflict involving the US, Israel and Iran has kept concerns over energy supplies elevated. On Sunday, the Iran-aligned Houthi movement claimed responsibility for an attack on a Saudi Arabian oil refinery. Multiple attacks on commercial shipping in the Gulf and near the Strait of Hormuz were also reported over the weekend.
The Strait of Hormuz is a key global oil transit route, making any disruption to shipping in the region a potential risk to international crude supplies.
Meanwhile, disagreements over fossil fuels continued at the global climate summit COP31 in Turkey. Talks collapsed on Sunday after participating nations failed to reach an agreement on including a reference to phasing out fossil fuels in the final text. It was the first such breakdown at the summit since 2009.
Saudi Arabia and other major oil-producing countries have maintained that fossil fuels will remain part of the global economy for the foreseeable future. Observers at the summit said these countries lobbied to keep references to fossil fuels out of the final document. The Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) had also defended fossil fuel use at the summit.
Meanwhile, OPEC and its allies, collectively known as OPEC+, are scheduled to hold a series of meetings on November 29 to decide their oil production policy for 2027. The group includes Russia and other major oil-producing nations.
Foreign inflows support rupee, government bonds; oil prices and US yields in focus
Strong foreign investment inflows are expected to support the Indian rupee and government bonds during the holiday-shortened week, with crude oil prices and US Treasury yields likely to remain key factors influencing domestic markets.
The Indian rupee closed at 92.67 against the US dollar on Friday, strengthening past the psychologically important 93-per-dollar mark for the first time since April. The currency gained 1.7% during the week.
Government bonds also recorded gains, with the benchmark 10-year bond yield declining 12 basis points last week to 7.1868%. It marked the yield's third weekly decline in four weeks. Traders expect the benchmark yield to trade in the range of 7.10% to 7.25% this week. Bond prices move inversely to yields.
The improvement in domestic financial markets has been supported by a shift in global investment flows away from AI-related stocks amid a deepening selloff in technology shares. India's relatively insulated equity markets have attracted foreign investment worth a record $12 billion, supporting the rupee and increasing demand for fixed-income assets.
The shift has also prompted investors to unwind bearish positions on the rupee. Foreign investors turned net buyers of Indian bonds in November after three consecutive months of selling, purchasing nearly $1.2 billion worth of bonds in the first three weeks of the month.
Lower crude oil prices and declining US Treasury yields have further supported the domestic market, offsetting concerns over a potentially more hawkish stance by the US Federal Reserve.
"Indian assets have benefited from a broader rotation away from AI-related exposures, alongside lower oil prices, which helped improve the macro backdrop and supported sentiment. These will be important drivers going forward also," said Shamaila Khan, head of fixed income for emerging markets and Asia-Pacific at UBS Asset Management.
A trader at a private bank said continued foreign investment inflows could support the rupee in the coming days. Market participants will also watch for signs of intervention by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), particularly the levels at which it may step in to replenish its foreign exchange reserves.
Norbert Ling, head of fixed income portfolio management for Asia-Pacific at Invesco, said Indian government bonds were benefiting from attractive carry, resilient domestic fundamentals and the possibility of inclusion in the Bloomberg Global Aggregate Index.
However, market participants remain cautious about the outlook, with inflation, crude oil prices and central bank decisions likely to influence investor sentiment.
Attention will turn to US personal consumption expenditures (PCE) inflation data due on Wednesday, followed by the RBI's monetary policy decision on December 4 and the US Federal Reserve's meeting on December 9.
Markets expect both central banks to raise interest rates by 25 basis points. However, an increase in expectations of a larger rate hike by the Fed could put pressure on Indian financial assets.
Ling cautioned that inflation remained above the RBI's tolerance band and that crude oil prices, despite their recent decline, remained vulnerable to renewed geopolitical tensions.
"The INR has stabilized and strengthened amid improving equity inflows, partly reflecting a rotation away from AI-related stocks, but the durability of this trend remains uncertain."

Gold, silver price outlook

Explaining the decline in domestic 
gold prices

Statements by Federal Reserve officials signalling a more hawkish approach have undermined demand for precious metals, as investors factor in the possibility of interest rates remaining elevated. The widespread decline in artificial intelligence-linked stocks has added to the selling pressure.
Silver has also been hit by weakness across the industrial metals segment, with copper and zinc recording particularly sharp declines, Mer pointed out.
According to him, the sell-off in equities prompted investors to liquidate bullion holdings as well, while demand for safe-haven bonds increased.

stories.headline: Anthropic IPO: Tracing an ‘unusual’ AI company’s race to the top
stories.deck: Set up as a Public Benefit Corporation, Anthropic warns that AI could be dangerous, yet races to build the most powerful models. Charts and a timeline unpack the journey and contradictions of the AI company behind the largest-ever IPO
stories.bodyText:
Minutes before Anthropic, the maker of Claude, began trading on Nasdaq on November 19, its co-founder and president Daniela Amodei opened her short speech by calling it an “unusual” company, one many even call “weird”.
Founded in May 2021 by seven former OpenAI employees who left over what they saw as a culture that did not put AI safety and alignment first, Anthropic is registered as a Public Benefit Corporation (PBC), a structure that legally binds the company to weigh public benefit alongside profit.
Its CEO Dario Amodei has consistently warned about the existential risks of misaligned AI models and pushed for regulation and a slowdown in the race to build frontier models. Rivals and some critics, however, have called this posturing. The provocatively titled “MisAnthropic Statement”, released on the eve of the IPO and signed by a few prominent figures from different fields, said Anthropic was not a safe AI company and urged rejection of its “reckless attempt to amass power in the name of the greater good”.
The charts and timeline below trace the unconventional journey of a company seen as a harbinger of everything unusual unfolding in the AI zeitgeist.
Anthropic raised $81.3 billion despite listing during a market slump — with many beginning to wonder whether the ballooning investments in AI were a bubble — and against the backdrop of the Republican rout in the U.S. midterms and the Nvidia scandal. It broke the record for the largest-ever IPO, set by Elon Musk’s SpaceX just five months earlier in a more bullish market.

briefs.headline: Harvesting gains tax efficiently
briefs.deck: Accumulating large gains in equity investments is risky as markets could tank, wiping out the gains; but realising all gains is also risky; allow unrealised gains in equity to compound for the goal
briefs.bodyText:
High net worth individuals are tax-aware investors. That is, their investment decisions are primarily driven by expected after-tax returns on an investment. Mass-affluent investors invest to achieve life goals. They incidentally take advantage of simple tax breaks available under the Income Tax Act. Here, we look at one such tax break— ₹1.25 lakh exemption for long-term capital gains.
Accumulating large gains in equity investments is risky as the market could tank, wiping out the gains. But realising all the gains is just as risky! Why? You must allow unrealised gains in equity portfolio to compound over time horizon for the goal. Otherwise, your portfolio will not accumulate the amount needed to achieve a goal. This causes a dilemma. You risk losing the unrealised gains if the market crashes. And, you risk not achieving goal if you realise all the gains. So, what next?
